advice: Measure the machine while your workload is stopped, then subtract that idle draw from your readings.
detail: An idle machine still uses power. SWEnergy's workstation drew 51.69 W of CPU power with nothing running, and removing it left only the agent's share.

advice: Track your workload by its process ID so other software on the same machine isn't counted against you.
detail: The Watts and Debts protocol follows the model server by its PID and subtracts its energy from the total to get the framework's own cost.

advice: On machines where you can't read energy counters, such as many VMs, use runtime and output tokens as stand-ins.
detail: In SWEnergy's agent runs, energy closely tracked wall-clock duration (R = 0.89) and output tokens (R = 0.88). Memory use showed almost no correlation.

advice: CPU and GPU counters leave out memory and storage, so read their totals as a partial cost.
detail: RAPL and NVML report processor and graphics energy only. Their totals are not what the machine draws from the wall.

advice: Compare versions on the same machine with the same tool, because absolute joules don't carry over between setups.
detail: pyRAPL gives estimates tuned to Intel hardware. Harmonica lists portable measurement across operating systems and virtual machines as an open problem.

advice: Decide between two versions using the average of several runs.
detail: Single readings are noisy. EnCoDe repeated each measurement 10 times and dropped outliers, after which over 90% of code blocks varied by less than 10%.

advice: Start your search for energy hotspots with loop-heavy and deeply nested blocks.
detail: Across more than 18,000 Python programs, loop count and nesting depth both correlated with block energy. Each link is weak by itself, so use them to decide where to look first.

advice: Don't treat cyclomatic complexity or code size as a stand-in for energy cost.
detail: Complexity metrics alone predicted energy tiers with 51% accuracy, close to chance. Energy came from how many code features combine.

advice: Use static energy estimation to shortlist likely hotspots before running anything, then measure the ones it flags.
detail: Models trained on 33 static code features placed blocks in the right energy tier 80.6% of the time. They rank hotspots well but don't give exact joules.

advice: Measure an agent framework's energy before adopting it, since architecture alone changed usage by up to 9×.
detail: With the same model and hardware, AutoCodeRover used 9.4× more energy per run than OpenHands.

advice: Count energy per task the agent actually completed, since a low-energy run may simply have given up early.
detail: Small-model agents resolved almost no issues. Some of the cheapest runs stopped as soon as the prompt exceeded the model's token limit.

advice: Stop or change strategy when an agent repeats the same failing action.
detail: Small models kept resubmitting the same failing test script, and none of the frameworks noticed the repetition.

advice: Trim tool output before it reaches the model's context window.
detail: Broad grep commands returned huge unfiltered outputs that filled a 32K context and made the agent lose track of its task.

advice: Gate every agent-generated patch on your CI build and tests, whatever the agent reports.
detail: Frameworks reported success for destructive patches, including one that replaced a 2,000-line file with a single invalid line.

advice: Keep both light and heavy models available and serve the lightest one that meets your accuracy target.
detail: HarmonE kept 95% of the heavy model's accuracy while using 45.5% of its energy, and inference time dropped by 53%.

advice: Check each candidate model's energy cost before defaulting to the most accurate one.
detail: For traffic forecasting, an LSTM reached R² 0.917 against an SVM's 0.821 but used about 8.4× the energy.

advice: Don't expect savings from swapping a small model into an agent framework built for large ones.
detail: SWEnergy found the swap ineffective and often counterproductive, because current frameworks assume a capable reasoning engine.

advice: Measure before assuming a smaller model saves energy inside an agent loop.
detail: In two of four frameworks, Qwen-3 1.7B used more tokens and energy than the larger Gemma-3 4B.

advice: Count runtime and energy when costing a local model, as well as the API fees you avoid.
detail: Local runs had no API fees, yet some configurations averaged 24 to 27 minutes per issue.

advice: Retrain when you detect data drift instead of on a fixed schedule.
detail: Drift-triggered retraining used 54.5% less energy than an LSTM retrained at fixed intervals.

advice: Before scheduling regular retraining of a heavy model, check that the accuracy gain justifies the energy.
detail: Periodic retraining added about 38% more energy to an LSTM for an R² gain of 0.008.

advice: Store each model with the data distribution it was trained on, and reuse it when that distribution comes back.
detail: HarmonE looks for a matching past model before retraining, which avoids repeat work when familiar patterns return.

advice: Pair model switching with selective retraining, because switching alone keeps falling back to the heaviest model.
detail: Switching without retraining used more energy than HarmonE (24.3 vs 20.6 mJ) and still fell short of the heavy model's accuracy.

advice: Set measurable energy and accuracy thresholds at design time and let them trigger adaptations.
detail: HarmonE turns sustainability goals into concrete limits, for example a maximum drift score before retraining starts.

advice: Monitor energy in production next to accuracy.
detail: HarmonE's monitor combines accuracy and normalised energy into one weighted score, and tracks data drift alongside it.

advice: Smooth metrics and allow a tolerance band so brief spikes don't trigger costly adaptations.
detail: HarmonE made 12 adaptations in a run, compared with 17 for model switching with periodic retraining.

advice: Expect a lightweight monitor-and-adapt loop to cost very little energy.
detail: HarmonE's adaptation loop accounted for 1.37% of total energy use.

advice: Keep adaptation logic in its own control layer, outside your training and inference code.
detail: Harmonica wraps existing ML pipelines with an adaptation loop and leaves their training and serving code unchanged.

advice: Compare adaptive approaches against static and fixed-retraining baselines on identical data splits.
detail: HarmonE compared nine approaches on the same splits. That comparison showed switching without retraining drifting toward the heavy LSTM.

advice: Inject controlled drift that recurs, so the experiment tests both drift detection and model reuse.
detail: HarmonE applied the same scale-and-shift transformation to two test segments, so the data diverges and later returns to a pattern the system has seen.

advice: Hold the hardware and model settings fixed, and run each trial on an otherwise idle machine.
detail: SWEnergy ran every configuration in FP16 with a 32K context on one dedicated workstation, with each run isolated from other work.

advice: Use a representative benchmark subset if that is what makes repeated runs affordable.
detail: SWE-bench Verified Mini has 50 tasks and takes about 5 GB instead of 130 GB. It let SWEnergy repeat every configuration three times, 1,200 runs in total.

advice: Fix temperature and seed, and do warm-up runs before you start measuring.
detail: The Watts and Debts protocol sets temperature 0.0 and seed 42. Two warm-up runs remove cold-start bias before any trial is recorded.

advice: Replicate on more than one hardware configuration and claim only the effects that hold on all of them.
detail: The study plans three machines with different CPU generations and GPUs, and counts a hypothesis as supported only if every machine agrees.

advice: Run feature-group ablations before claiming that any single metric explains energy.
detail: In EnCoDe, complexity metrics alone reached R² = 0.067, and no single feature group matched the full model.

advice: Compare Pearson with rank correlations, and check strong correlations against model feature importance.
detail: Rank correlations ran well above Pearson, which points to largely non-linear relationships. One feature with high rank correlation added little to prediction.

advice: For code that runs in under a millisecond, repeat it in a loop and align the measurement window to counter updates.
detail: Single RAPL readings below 1 ms varied by over 110% or read zero. The full PowerLens protocol brought over 90% of blocks under 10% variation.

advice: Fix the CPU frequency and pin the process to one core before measuring small blocks.
detail: PowerLens also disables Turbo Boost and stops background processes. The paper notes that single-core pinning hides multi-threading effects.

advice: Check fine-grained energy measurements against a whole-program measurement tool.
detail: Summed block-level readings closely matched pyRAPL's program-level energy, with lower variance.

advice: Record each machine's idle power draw and subtract it from every energy trace you report.
detail: SWEnergy measured 51.69 W CPU and 2.70 W GPU at idle and removed both from its RAPL and NVML traces.

advice: Attribute energy by process ID to separate the inference server from the framework you are studying.
detail: Watts and Debts plans to compute framework energy as total energy minus the model server's energy, tracked by its PID.

advice: State which components your energy tools cover, and don't call CPU plus GPU totals whole-system energy.
detail: RAPL and NVML leave out RAM and storage, so their totals fall short of wall-plug energy.

advice: Measure the energy of your adaptation or monitoring logic itself.
detail: HarmonE's MAPE-K loop took 17.9 ms per invocation and accounted for 1.37% of total system energy.

advice: Repeat each configuration several times with cooldown gaps between runs before averaging energy.
detail: HarmonE used five independent runs with 20-minute cooldowns so temperature and background load could settle.

advice: Report energy alongside task success, and verify success independently of the system under test.
detail: The most frugal framework resolved 0% of tasks, and some reported successes were destructive patches.

advice: Don't generalise per-success energy from a handful of successes.
detail: With near-zero resolution rates, SWEnergy notes that its conclusions about failed runs are far more robust than those about successful ones.

advice: If an LLM helps analyse your logs, hand-check a random sample and publish the raw logs.
detail: SWEnergy used an LLM to classify failure modes. Two authors verified a random sample, and the full logs are in the replication package.

advice: Pre-register hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting data, for example as a registered report.
detail: Watts and Debts fixed its hypotheses and Spearman tests in advance through the ESEM registered reports track.

advice: With few units of analysis, set a minimum effect size in advance and judge results by magnitude rather than p-values.
detail: With only five frameworks to compare, the study pre-specifies ρ ≥ 0.50 as the smallest effect worth reporting.

advice: When energy values span orders of magnitude, report both absolute and relative error.
detail: EnCoDe's best regressor reached R² = 0.755 yet had MAPE above 170%, mostly from very low-energy blocks.

advice: Report the energy cost of your prediction model next to its accuracy.
detail: A Random Forest classifier used 0.373 J against XGBoost's 0.022 J and was also slightly less accurate.

advice: Report energy, accuracy, latency and number of adaptations side by side.
detail: HarmonE's results table gives all four for every approach, with an energy-versus-error plot alongside.

advice: Name your energy tool's hardware limits and the exact platform, and release your code and configurations.
detail: HarmonE notes that pyRAPL works only on Intel processors and lists its full platform. Its code and configurations are public.

advice: Extend block-level energy estimation to varying input sizes and multi-threaded code.
detail: EnCoDe does not model how energy scales with input, and it pins measurement to a single core.

advice: Build energy measurement that works across operating systems and virtualised hardware.
detail: Harmonica calls portable energy instrumentation an open challenge, since pyRAPL only supports Intel processors.

advice: Test sustainability-aware MLOps beyond time series, especially in systems built on language models.
detail: HarmonE was evaluated on one traffic-forecasting task. Its authors point to LLM and SLM systems, where model-selection trade-offs are sharper.

advice: Design agent frameworks that manage small models' weaknesses, for example by detecting loops and checking patches independently.
detail: SWEnergy argues that current frameworks are passive orchestrators built for capable LLMs.

advice: Test whether self-admitted technical debt predicts which agent frameworks use the most energy.
detail: Watts and Debts sets out to test this across five frameworks. Results are not in yet.
